pages.title: About
pages.content:
About Kyukyu College

Kyukyu College was founded in 2011 at 41 Wexford Lane in Northmere by Dr. Ruth Adeyemi-Holm, a former emergency physician, and two station paramedics. It teaches one thing: the work that happens before the hospital.

Each intake is limited to twenty-four students, taught in scenarios first with the theory behind them, at one instructor to eight students in the skills lab. Every instructor still works shifts on an ambulance.

The building holds two classrooms, a skills lab with two ambulance-body simulators and a drill hall. Fuller pages on the course, ride-along placements, admissions and faculty follow in the next release of this sample content.

posts.title: The night shift I stopped counting
posts.excerpt: Aiyana Clarke, class of 2023, on the move from the simulator to her first call.
posts.content:
Aiyana Clarke graduated in 2023 and now works on a city ambulance crew. She remembers the first night shift she did not count down to the end of.

In the skills lab the manikin never cried and the lights never changed. On the road, her mentor showed her how to slow her own voice first, and then everything else slowed with it.

“The course teaches you the steps,” she says. “The placement teaches you the order they come in when nobody is waiting for you to finish.”

posts.title: Starting at forty-one
posts.excerpt: Daniel Weiss joined after twelve years in warehouse work.
posts.content:
Daniel Weiss spent twelve years in warehouse work before he applied. The fitness assessment worried him less than the pharmacology.

He took the Foundation Term first, then the Paramedic Diploma, and studies on a bench outside the college between classes.

His advice to anyone considering a second career: “Come to an open evening, ask the instructors what their week looks like, and decide after that.”

posts.title: Why we time every compression
posts.excerpt: Tomás Arriaga on stopwatches, feedback lights and the first eight minutes.
posts.content:
Tomás Arriaga, our lead clinical instructor, has been a paramedic for eighteen years. In the skills lab every compression drill is timed with a stopwatch while a second student watches the manikin’s feedback light.

“Rate is a habit before it is a skill,” he says. “If a student can feel two minutes in their hands, they can do it on the worst night of their year.”

Every drill ends with a debrief: what the numbers were, and what the student noticed.

posts.title: Open evening dates for spring
posts.excerpt: Open evenings run on the first Thursday of each month.
posts.content:
Open evenings run on the first Thursday of every month from 18:00 to 20:00 at 41 Wexford Lane, Northmere.

Visitors tour the skills lab, see the ambulance-body simulators and talk to instructors and the admissions office.

posts.title: New ambulance-body simulator in the skills lab
posts.excerpt: A second ambulance-body simulator joins the skills lab.
posts.content:
The skills lab now has two ambulance-body simulators, so a full group of eight students can rehearse loading and treating a patient in a confined space at the same time.

Lab ratios stay at one instructor to eight students.

posts.title: February intake: applications open
posts.excerpt: Apply by 30 September for the February intake; places are limited to 24.
posts.content:
Applications for the February intake follow the same steps as September: written test, fitness and manual-handling assessment, interview, then health and background checks.

There are twenty-four places in each intake. The application fee is $60.
